pack.description: Spelling traps: common academic and campus words that are easy to misspell, especially for French speakers, with the point to watch. Useful for Complete the Words and for writing tasks.
pack.selection_note: Internal selection of frequently misspelled words, with a focus on French interference; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: to provide a place for someone to stay or enough space for something; or to adapt to a need
entries.example_academic: The new hall can accommodate up to four hundred students.
entries.example_spoken: The office accommodated my request to change rooms.
entries.spelling_trap: double c and double m: a-cc-o-mm-odate

entries.definition: needed in order to do something or for something to happen
entries.example_academic: Oxygen is necessary for the reaction to take place.
entries.example_spoken: It isn't necessary to print the slides.
entries.spelling_trap: one c, double s, as in French "nécessaire": ne-c-e-ss-ary

entries.definition: not joined to or connected with something else; different
entries.example_academic: The two findings were published in separate articles.
entries.example_spoken: We have separate rooms but share a kitchen.
entries.spelling_trap: the middle vowel is a, not e: sep-a-rate (not "seperate")

entries.definition: without any doubt; certainly
entries.example_academic: The manuscript was definitely produced before the fire of 1666.
entries.example_spoken: I'm definitely coming to the review session.
entries.spelling_trap: contains "finite": de-finite-ly (not "definately")

entries.definition: to get or be given something
entries.example_academic: Participants received a small payment for completing the survey.
entries.example_spoken: Did you receive my email yesterday?
entries.spelling_trap: e before i after c: re-cei-ve

entries.definition: the group of people who officially control and run a country or region
entries.example_academic: The government introduced a tax on sugary drinks.
entries.example_spoken: The government is changing the visa rules again.
entries.spelling_trap: keep the n of "govern", and o not ou as in French: govern-ment

entries.definition: the natural world of land, air, water, plants and animals; or the conditions around a person
entries.example_academic: Plastic waste persists in the environment for centuries.
entries.example_spoken: I work better in a quiet environment.
entries.spelling_trap: one n before -ment (French "environnement" has two) and no e: environ-ment

entries.definition: not controlled or helped by other people or things; separate
entries.example_academic: An independent laboratory confirmed the original measurements.
entries.example_spoken: She's been financially independent since she was eighteen.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -ent, not -ant as in French "indépendant"

entries.definition: to say that something is good or suitable, or to advise someone to do something
entries.example_academic: The panel recommends that funding be extended for two years.
entries.example_spoken: Can you recommend a good dictionary?
entries.spelling_trap: one c, double m: re-c-o-mm-end

entries.definition: now or without any delay
entries.example_academic: Symptoms appear almost immediately after exposure.
entries.example_spoken: Call me immediately if the file doesn't open.
entries.spelling_trap: double m, and keep the e of "immediate" before -ly: i-mm-ediat-e-ly

entries.definition: the details of where a person lives or works, or where an email can be sent
entries.example_academic: Each respondent was identified by an address rather than by a name.
entries.example_spoken: What's your new address? I'll send you the form.
entries.spelling_trap: double d, unlike French "adresse": a-dd-ress

entries.definition: a set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a building
entries.example_academic: Rents for a one-bedroom apartment rose by a third in five years.
entries.example_spoken: We found an apartment ten minutes from campus.
entries.spelling_trap: one p and no e before -ment, unlike French "appartement": a-p-art-ment

entries.definition: making you feel physically relaxed; or having no worries about a situation
entries.example_academic: Participants were seated in a comfortable room with natural light.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not comfortable speaking in front of the whole class yet.
entries.spelling_trap: m, not n as in French "confortable": co-m-fortable

entries.definition: having the job of dealing with something; or being the cause of something
entries.example_academic: A single gene is responsible for the difference in color.
entries.example_spoken: Who's responsible for booking the room?
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -ible, not -able as in French "responsable"

entries.definition: the process of growing, changing or becoming more advanced; or a new event
entries.example_academic: The development of writing transformed the administration of early states.
entries.example_spoken: Any new developments with your application?
entries.spelling_trap: one p and no e before -ment, unlike French "développement": develop-ment

entries.definition: written works such as novels, plays and poems; or everything published on a subject
entries.example_academic: The literature on climate adaptation has grown rapidly in the past decade.
entries.example_spoken: I'm taking a course on American literature.
entries.spelling_trap: one t, unlike French "littérature": li-t-erature

entries.definition: the first part of something, or the time when it starts
entries.example_academic: At the beginning of the century, most of the population lived in villages.
entries.example_spoken: I missed the beginning of the lecture.
entries.spelling_trap: double n: begi-nn-ing

entries.definition: something that happens, or the fact of something happening
entries.example_academic: Flooding is a regular occurrence in the lower valley.
entries.example_spoken: Power cuts are a common occurrence in that building.
entries.spelling_trap: double c, double r, ending -ence: o-cc-u-rr-ence

entries.definition: the work of keeping something in good condition
entries.example_academic: Poor maintenance of the canals led to a decline in harvests.
entries.example_spoken: I called maintenance about the broken heater.
entries.spelling_trap: -ten-, not -tain-: main-ten-ance (not "maintainance")

entries.definition: the way in which a word or language is spoken
entries.example_academic: Spelling reforms rarely keep pace with changes in pronunciation.
entries.example_spoken: My pronunciation of "th" still needs work.
entries.spelling_trap: -nun-, not -noun-: pro-nun-ciation (the verb is "pronounce")

entries.definition: a special right or advantage that only some people have
entries.example_academic: Access to higher education was long a privilege of the wealthy.
entries.example_spoken: It's a privilege to work with such a good team.
entries.spelling_trap: two i's, then e, and no d: priv-i-lege (not "priviledge")

entries.definition: to make something seem larger, better or worse than it really is
entries.example_academic: Early reports exaggerated the scale of the damage.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not exaggerating; the line went around the building.
entries.spelling_trap: double g, unlike French "exagérer": exa-gg-erate

entries.definition: letters or emails that people write to each other; or a close similarity between two things
entries.example_academic: The correspondence between the two scientists fills three volumes.
entries.example_spoken: All correspondence about the lease should go to the housing office.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -ence, not -ance as in French "correspondance"

entries.definition: to make someone feel ashamed, nervous or uncomfortable in front of others
entries.example_academic: The leaked report embarrassed the ministry.
entries.example_spoken: I didn't mean to embarrass you in front of the class.
entries.spelling_trap: double r and double s: emba-rr-a-ss

entries.definition: a firm promise that something will happen or be done; or a written promise to repair or replace a product
entries.example_academic: Legal reforms provided a guarantee of property rights.
entries.example_spoken: There's no guarantee that we'll get the room.
entries.spelling_trap: starts with gua- and ends in double e, unlike French "garantie": g-u-arant-ee

entries.definition: the part of your mind that tells you whether what you are doing is right or wrong
entries.example_academic: The essay examines the conflict between law and individual conscience.
entries.example_spoken: My conscience wouldn't let me copy his answers.
entries.spelling_trap: contains "science": con-science; do not confuse with "conscious" (aware)

entries.definition: a regular repeated pattern of sounds or movements
entries.example_academic: The rhythm of English speech depends on the alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables.
entries.example_spoken: I can't dance; I have no sense of rhythm.
entries.spelling_trap: two h's and no vowel but y: r-h-y-t-h-m (French "rythme" has one h)

entries.definition: a written list of questions used to collect information from people
entries.example_academic: Each household completed a questionnaire on its energy use.
entries.example_spoken: It takes five minutes to fill out the questionnaire.
entries.spelling_trap: double n and final -aire: questio-nn-aire

entries.definition: running side by side at the same distance apart; or similar and happening at the same time
entries.example_academic: The two rivers follow parallel courses for nearly a hundred kilometers.
entries.example_spoken: The streets are parallel, so you can take either one.
entries.spelling_trap: double l in the middle, single l at the end: para-ll-e-l

entries.definition: continued effort to do something despite difficulty or delay
entries.example_academic: The discovery was the result of perseverance rather than sudden insight.
entries.example_spoken: Learning a language takes perseverance more than talent.
entries.spelling_trap: -sever- in the middle and -ance at the end: per-sever-ance

entries.definition: so small or unimportant that it is not worth considering
entries.example_academic: The effect on prices was negligible in the first year.
entries.example_spoken: The difference in cost is negligible, so pick the one you like.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -igible (French "négligeable" has -eable): negl-ig-ible

entries.definition: easy to see or become aware of
entries.example_academic: There was a noticeable improvement in reading scores after the program.
entries.example_spoken: There's a noticeable difference since you started practicing.
entries.spelling_trap: keep the e of "notice" before -able: notic-e-able

entries.definition: so important or useful that it is impossible to manage without it
entries.example_academic: Reliable census data are indispensable for planning public services.
entries.example_spoken: A good calendar app is indispensable during exam season.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -able, not -ible: indispens-able

entries.definition: the level at which something starts to happen or change
entries.example_academic: Above a certain threshold, the reaction becomes self-sustaining.
entries.example_spoken: My threshold for noise is pretty low when I'm studying.
entries.spelling_trap: only one h in the middle: thres-hold (not "threshhold")

entries.definition: a system of government or management with many officials and complicated rules
entries.example_academic: The expansion of the bureaucracy required a new class of literate officials.
entries.example_spoken: There's so much bureaucracy just to change one course.
entries.spelling_trap: starts with "bureau" and ends in -cracy, not -cratie: bureau-cracy

entries.definition: an opinion that all or most members of a group agree with
entries.example_academic: There is a broad consensus that the climate is warming.
entries.example_spoken: There's no consensus in our group about the topic.
entries.spelling_trap: s, not c, in the middle (related to "consent", not "census"): con-s-ensus

entries.definition: a situation in which a difficult choice has to be made between two or more options
entries.example_academic: Policymakers face a dilemma between controlling prices and supporting growth.
entries.example_spoken: I'm in a dilemma: take the job or finish my degree first.
entries.spelling_trap: double m and final a: dile-mm-a (not "dilemna")

entries.definition: taking care to do your work well and thoroughly
entries.example_academic: A conscientious observer, she recorded the weather three times a day for forty years.
entries.example_spoken: He's the most conscientious person in our group; he checks everything twice.
entries.spelling_trap: conscience with -tious instead of -ce: con-sci-en-tious

entries.definition: consisting of many different kinds of things that are not easily grouped together
entries.example_academic: The final box contained miscellaneous papers, including bills and invitations.
entries.example_spoken: I keep a folder for miscellaneous notes.
entries.spelling_trap: sc, double l, and -eous at the end: mi-sc-e-ll-an-eous

entries.definition: enjoying playing tricks and causing small trouble, usually in a playful way
entries.example_academic: The narrator adopts a mischievous tone that undermines the official version of events.
entries.example_spoken: He gave me a mischievous smile and hid my notes.
entries.spelling_trap: three syllables, no i after the v: mis-chie-vous (not "mischievious")

entries.definition: to take the place of something older or less effective
entries.example_academic: The new regulations supersede all earlier guidelines.
entries.example_spoken: This version of the syllabus supersedes the one from August.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -sede with an s, not -cede: super-sede

entries.definition: an unusual habit or feature that belongs to one particular person or thing
entries.example_academic: The spelling reflects the idiosyncrasies of a single scribe.
entries.example_spoken: One of his idiosyncrasies is writing everything in green ink.
entries.spelling_trap: ends in -asy, not -acy: idio-syn-crasy

entries.definition: the careful watching of a person or place, especially by the police or the state
entries.example_academic: The expansion of digital surveillance has raised concerns about privacy.
entries.example_spoken: The lab is under video surveillance at night.
entries.spelling_trap: same spelling as in French: sur-veill-ance (ei, double l)

entries.definition: a person who knows a great deal about art, food, music or another subject and can judge its quality
entries.example_academic: The collection was assembled by a connoisseur of early printed maps.
entries.example_spoken: He thinks he's a coffee connoisseur.
entries.spelling_trap: oi, not ai as in modern French "connaisseur", with double n and double s: co-nn-oi-ss-eur

entries.definition: extremely small in size or amount
entries.example_academic: The margin of error is minuscule compared with the size of the effect.
entries.example_spoken: My room is minuscule, but it's close to campus.
entries.spelling_trap: u after the n (think "minus", not "mini"): min-u-scule
